children: 0801 ET - The euro could recover against the dollar next year if energy prices ease, Commerzbank's Thu Lan Nguyen says in a note. Energy prices should fall in coming months, relieving pressure on European bond markets, she says. Lower energy prices would also likely lead to a correction in elevated interest-rate rise expectations for the U.S. and eurozone, she says. "We expect the dollar to suffer more from such a correction than the euro, not least because lower energy prices should improve the economic outlook for the euro-area by more than for the U.S." Commerzbank expects the euro to rise to $1.18 by December 2027, from $1.1212 currently.(renae.dyer@wsj.com)

0752 ET - Strong jobs and firmer pay data in the U.K. will probably make Bank of England Gov. Andrew Bailey's choice a little easier when deciding whether to raise interest rates at November's meeting, HSBC's Elizabeth Martins says. At the IMF meeting in Bangkok last week, he appeared not to have made up his mind, and the subdued labor market has been a key reason for policymakers' reticence thus far, she says in a note. "Even if [Wedenesday's] inflation data are soft, the pickup in pay growth and evidence of a more resilient economy point to increased risks of the energy shock leading to second-round effects," Martins says. HSBC forecasts a 25 basis-point hike to 4.0% on Nov. 5. (edward.frankl@wsj.com)

0751 ET - Sterling's reaction to the October 28 budget depends on whether the measures reinforce confidence in the government's fiscal approach, Nuveen's Laura Cooper says in a note. "A credible package should provide support, although the downside risks are greater if investors judge the measures insufficient." Nuveen expects a relatively restrained budget with limited additional spending and targeted tax increases aimed at rebuilding fiscal headroom.However, the Bank of England is unlikely to raise interest rates as much as markets expect, leaving sterling vulnerable to a potential repricing, she says. Sterling rises 0.2% to $1.3340 while the euro falls 0.3% to a near 17-month low of 0.8397 pounds after improved U.K. employment data, according to LSEG. (renae.dyer@wsj.com)

0713 ET - The U.K.'s latest jobs data reinforces that view that there has been some stabilization in the jobs market, Deutsche Bank's Sanjay Raja says in a note. The unemployment rate fell to 4.7%, its lowest rate since July 2025, despite consensus expectations for it to rise. "Stronger growth has now finally landed with the labor market. And limited budget speculation has meant that firms are cautiously hiring," he says. This is good news for the government, as more workers will mean more tax receipts. However, for the Bank of England, the data speaks to a labor market that has less slack than previously envisaged, Raja notes. "The case for insurance hikes, in our minds, is growing especially with CPI on course to top 4% in the coming months." (edward.frankl@wsj.com)

0541 ET - Shorter-dated U.K. government bonds, or gilts, look attractive as expectations for Bank of England interest-rate rises are overdone, Nuveen's Laura Cooper says in a note. "For gilt investors, we think the bigger risk is that markets have priced in too much tightening, not too little fiscal restraint." The BOE could deliver an insurance rate increase in November but that move could be reversed in 2027 as the drag on growth builds, she says. Nuveen favors five-year gilts, which offer exposure to a potential repricing of BOE expectations without the same sensitivity to fiscal risks and term premium further out the curve if the October 28 budget disappoints. The five-year gilt yield falls 2.3 basis points to 5.021%, Tradeweb data show. (renae.dyer@wsj.com)

0533 ET - U.S. Treasurys could regain their diversification value if an AI-led market correction deepens, say Julius Baer analysts in a note. While stock-bond correlations have risen, the bank says a sharper AI downturn would resemble a traditional negative demand shock, as weaker data-center investment, falling equity wealth and softer hiring weigh on consumption and business spending. Historically, U.S. 10-year Treasurys delivered positive returns during equity drawdowns between 2000 and 2020, the bank notes. Julius Baer says recent correlation doesn't necessarily undermine Treasurys' hedging potential, and sees intermediate-duration U.S. government bonds as an effective portfolio hedge. (jiahui.huang@wsj.com; @ivy_jiahuihuang)

0522 ET - The Brazilian real could strengthen if Senator Flavio Bolsonaro wins the country's runoff presidential election on Sunday, Commerzbank's Norman Liebke says in a note. "Bolsonaro has announced greater fiscal consolidation and a generally more market-oriented economic policy in an effort to rein in Brazil's high debt ratio of almost 83% of GDP." While the real is likely to rise in the short-term, how long this appreciation lasts will depend on which fiscal measures Bolsonaro announces and is actually able to implement, he says. In the first round on voting on October 4, Bolsonaro secured a narrow lead over incumbent President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva. The dollar rises 0.1% to 5.0366 real. (renae.dyer@wsj.com)

0517 ET - Gulf economies face pressure from disruptions to fertilizer supply chains and their reliance on imported food as the Strait of Hormuz conflict continues, S&P Global Ratings says. The region is exposed both as an energy and fertilizer supplier and as a major food importer. Higher nitrogen and phosphate prices relative to agricultural commodity prices have weakened fertilizer affordability globally, while China's export restrictions and a sulfur shortage continue to constrain supplies. S&P expects pressure on fertilizer markets to persist through the rest of 2026, with only gradual improvement in 2027, raising concerns about food costs and agricultural demand. (farhan.rafid@wsj.com)

0515 ET - Dubai's economy contracted 2.3% in real terms in the first half of 2026, with gross domestic product falling to 473 billion dirhams ($128.8 billion) from 484 billion dirhams a year earlier, according to the Dubai Data and Statistics Establishment. Financial and insurance activities grew 8.8%, accounting for 14% of GDP, up from 12.5% a year earlier. However, wholesale and retail trade contracted 6% in real terms, while transportation and storage declined 7.4% and real estate fell 2.5%. Construction grew 2.4%, while healthcare and social work activities expanded 14.3%. GDP at current prices rose 0.2% to 505 billion dirhams. (farhan.rafid@wsj.com)

0514 ET - China's stronger-than-expected 3Q growth rules out additional stimulus, BNP Paribas says in a research note. China's 3Q GDP rose 4.5% on year, accelerating from a 4.3% rise in 2Q. The reading outpaced both BNP Paribas's estimate of 4.3% and market consensus of 4.4%. "Further fiscal stimulus now unlikely," it says. A ministimulus package for 4Q has already been introduced to bridge any potential gap between underlying growth momentum and the annual target. "We believe current fiscal resources should be sufficient to support a mild pickup in growth in 4Q, and we maintain our annual growth forecast of 4.6%," the bank says. (tracy.qu@wsj.com)

0510 ET - Malaysia's inflation is expected to rise gradually toward the year end as higher input costs and elevated oil prices feed into consumer prices, Public Investment Bank analyst Sabrina Edora says in a note. She maintains her 2026 inflation forecast at 1.9%, with the 2027 projection at 2.3%. Targeted fuel subsidies and electricity-bill relief should cushion household costs through end-2026, while El Nino poses risks to food prices, she says. The 2,000 ringgit minimum wage from June 2027 could add to services inflation, although exemptions for some micro, small and medium-size enterprises may limit the impact, she adds. The economist expects Bank Negara Malaysia to keep its policy rate at 2.75% through the end of the year before a possible 25-basis point hike in 2027, depending on wage and inflation pressures. (yingxian.wong@wsj.com)

0503 ET - The People's Bank of China is likely to hold its policy rate steady for rest of 2026, BNP Paribas says in a research note, citing unabated pressure on banks' net interest margins. BNP Paribas points out that the new property policy provides nationwide interest-rate subsidy for commercial mortgage loans, rather than an outright mortgage-rate cut. This is likely to provide some relief to banks, it adds. "The shift from broad-based deflation to mild inflation and the potential for further interest-rate hikes from the U.S. Fed are likely to limit monetary easing, in our view," it adds. (tracy.qu@wsj.com)

title: Euro Could Recover if Energy Prices Eases — Market Talk
